activities.anchor: Time itself is the sensitive instrument
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the clock deep in the curve
activities.name: grDeepClockPredict

config.q: A clock sits near a one-solar-mass black hole's horizon; its twin sits far away. To the distant observer, what does the deep clock do?
choices: Ticks slightly faster — gravity boosts deep clocks
Runs slower, and at the horizon appears to freeze entirely
Runs at the same rate — gravity bends paths, not time
Slows a little, but never below half its far-away rate
config.why: Near the horizon a clock ticks at nearly zero compared with a distant observer — time is the sensitive instrument, and deep in the curve the geometry is exquisitely position-sensitive.

activities.caption: file each Earth-lab measurement by its instrument
activities.name: grEarthSort

config.prompt: Clocks, not forces, are the instruments — file each measurement:

items.label: a clock at sea level runs slower than one on a mountain
NIST, 2010: the rate difference between two clocks 33 cm apart vertically, resolved
the effect runs about one part in 10¹⁶ per metre of height
gravitational redshift: light climbing out of a potential well loses frequency
Pound–Rebka (1959): redshift confirmed across the 22.5 m Harvard tower

config.why: Near Earth, curvature is measurable in time — and weight turns out to be geometry's most personal manifestation.

activities.anchor: is the arena where general relativity met its first test
activities.caption: rebuild the 43-arcsecond story
activities.name: grMercuryOrder

config.prompt: Assemble the first great test, in order:
items: Newton's gravity gets the planets almost exactly right — almost
Mercury's perihelion drifts 43 arcseconds per century beyond every Newtonian correction — a discrepancy known since 1859
Einstein's 1915 calculation reproduces the 43 arcseconds exactly, with no tuning — 'beside himself with joyous excitement'
The mechanism: near the Sun, curvature slightly exceeds what an inverse-square force predicts, so the elliptical orbit's axis precesses
config.why: Any theory of gravity must first survive the Mercury-and-GPS gauntlet — general relativity has passed every probe, including Cassini's Shapiro-delay check to 2 parts in 100,000.

activities.anchor: the mass that sets the Solar System's geometry
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — the bending of starlight
activities.name: grBendEst

config.prompt: Light grazing the solar limb bends by α = 4GM/c²R. How many arcseconds is that?
config.why: Twice the 'Newtonian' value — half of which even Einstein's 1911 theory had given. Eddington's 1919 eclipse expeditions found the shift and made Einstein famous.
config.context: The bending is not 'gravity pulling on light' but light travelling straight through curved space — the angle is geometry.

activities.anchor: are general relativity's most dramatic territory
activities.caption: pair each stellar ending with what holds it up
activities.name: grCorpseMatch

config.prompt: The mass decides the fate — pair each ending with its physics:

pairs.right: electron degeneracy pressure — Earth-sized, teaspoon-tonne density
neutron degeneracy — city-sized, spinning, the pulsars Jocelyn Bell found in 1967
nothing holds: collapse passes the Schwarzschild radius, and every future-pointing path leads inward
two black holes of 36 and 29 solar masses merging 1.3 billion light-years away — the first direct hearing of spacetime ringing

config.why: The syllabus's 'life cycle of a star' is, in expert terms, a catalogue of gravitational collapse outcomes.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the field equation at full scale
activities.name: grCosmosCloze

config.text: Apply Einstein's equation to a universe that is uniform and isotropic, and the geometry must %%0%% — the Friedmann solutions, which Einstein initially resisted with a cosmological constant he later called his biggest %%1%%. Hubble's 1929 observations settled it. Cosmic expansion is not galaxies flying through space but %%2%% itself growing — the metric changing with time, with no centre and no edge.
config.hint: What Friedmann's solutions permit Einstein to dislike; the word he used in retrospect; what is actually growing.

activities.anchor: gravity in general relativity is a force that attracts
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's notes on weightlessness
activities.name: grForceSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's notes is wrong — click it:
lines: A falling object is in free fall, feeling nothing, tracing the straightest line available in curved spacetime.
What we call 'the force of gravity' standing on the ground is the floor's electromagnetic resistance — the atoms preventing you from following your geodesic.
The astronaut on the ISS is beyond gravity: Earth's pull there is essentially zero.
Gravity as a force is redefined out of existence — geodesics replace it.
config.correction: Earth's gravity at the ISS's orbit is about 90% of surface strength — she is finally unresisted, coasting along her geodesic, not beyond the pull.
config.why: There is no force to be beyond: the free-falling astronaut and the falling apple both feel nothing.

activities.anchor: the Universe is expanding into something
activities.caption: drag the divider — what cosmic expansion is and is not
activities.name: grExpandCompare

config.prompt: One phenomenon, two readings — drag to compare:

before.label: what it is NOT
before.text: Galaxies flying through space from a central explosion point — a centre, an edge, an outside point of view required. None of that is in the equations.

after.label: what it IS
after.text: An internal stretching of space: every galaxy recedes from every other, like dots on an inflating balloon whose surface is all there is. The Big Bang happened everywhere at once — 'where is the centre?' has the same status as 'what is north of the North Pole?'

config.why: Expansion is the metric changing with time — the curvature dynamics of the same field equation that runs stars and black holes.
